title: Strings: the weakest cell sets the pace

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is one current draining all six tanks equally, until the small tank empties first and turns red, driven backwards while the big tanks still hold charge, when you run the discharge on.
interactive.title: The string as tanks
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: Six lead-acid cells sit side by side in series. Each is drawn as a tank. Five tanks hold 100 Ah. The sixth is a faded cell that holds an example 80 Ah. A small-cell stepper sets it to 60, 70, 80, 90 or 100 Ah. One current arrow runs through all six, because a series string gives the current only one path. A mode switch picks Discharge, Charge or Float. On Discharge and Charge, the current is an example 10 A, and an hours scrubber runs from 0 to 12 hours. Each hour, every tank falls or rises by the same 10 Ah, whatever its size. On Discharge, the small tank empties first. Past empty, the other five drive the same current through it, so it is drawn red and reversed. The useful ampere-hours stop at the small cell's size, because the charge forced out past that point is not useful capacity. On Charge, all six start flat. The small tank fills first, then turns the current into heat and gas, drawn as bubbles. On Float, each tank shows its cell voltage. The charger holds the total at an example 2.23 V a cell, 13.38 V for six. A band on each cell runs from 2.18 to 2.33 V, 0.05 V below to 0.10 V above 2.23 V. An odd-cell slider sets the sixth cell from 2.03 to 2.43 V. The other five share the rest of 13.38 V equally, so the total never moves. The second card shows two strings of an example 10 mΩ in parallel sharing a 100 A load. A slider sets each string's cable from 1 to 10 mΩ. Both strings have the same emf on the same busbars, so each path loses the same volts. Each current is those volts over its path's resistance, so string A carries 100 × path B ÷ (path A + path B). The readouts are the useful ampere-hours, what the small cell holds, and string A's current. The last screens draw two 12 V blocks in series and in parallel.
interactive.ignores: Each tank's size is fixed. A real cell gives fewer ampere-hours at a higher current or in the cold, as lesson 3 showed. Charging is drawn ampere-hour for ampere-hour. A real recharge needs about a fifth more in than came out. The reversed cell is held at empty and drawn red. A real reversed cell may partly charge the wrong way round. A recharge must undo that first. On Float, the other five cells share the difference equally. Real cells each differ a little. The parallel card keeps both strings' voltages equal and fixed. Real strings drift as they discharge, and that moves the share over time. Time is sped up.

explain.text:
Cells joined in series make a [[string]]. One current flows through every cell. So each cell gives the same ampere-hours, hour by hour. The cell that holds the fewest runs out first, and then the string is finished. Charge the string from flat, and the same cell is full first. Either way, the weak cell is the one pushed too far.

Picture six cells as tanks. Five hold 100 Ah. One faded cell holds, say, 80 Ah. Draw 10 A from the string. The current has only one path, so every cell gives 10 Ah each hour. After 8 hours the small cell has given its 80 Ah and is empty. The big cells still hold 20 Ah each. But every amp must pass the empty cell to reach the load. So the string can reach that charge only by driving the empty cell backwards. Its volts fall away once the small cell is empty. So its useful capacity is 80 Ah, not 100.

Keep the load on, and the five strong cells push the same current through the empty one. It has nothing left to give. So the current drives it backwards, and its voltage turns round. This is [[cell reversal]]. It can leave the cell with a permanent short. In a long string, one cell is a small part of the total. So the total can look healthy while one cell is being reversed.

A deep discharge can leave every cell flat. Now charge the string from flat at 10 A, and the story runs the other way. After 8 hours the small cell is full. The other five still need 20 Ah each, so the current keeps flowing. The full cell cannot store it. So it turns the current into heat and gas. Kept up, that overcharge helps corrode its positive grid. An ordinary part-discharge from full is different. Every cell needs the same ampere-hours back, so they fill together. The weak cell gets ahead only from flat, or on float.

On float, the charger holds the total voltage. Say it is 2.23 V a cell, or 13.38 V for six. A weak cell can sit in overcharge. Its plates take no more charge, so its voltage climbs towards its gassing voltage. The total is fixed. So the strong cells share less and stay starved of charge.

Say each cell is allowed 0.05 V below to 0.10 V above its float voltage, as long as the total is right.[^2] For 2.23 V, that band runs from 2.18 to 2.33 V. Say the weak cell reads 2.38 V. The other five share what is left, 2.20 V each. The total still reads 13.38 V, because the charger holds it there. So the total cannot find a bad cell. Cell-by-cell readings can. That is how a battery can float at the right voltage and still fall short on a discharge test.

Strings can also sit side by side, in parallel. Their ampere-hours add, and the voltage stays the same. Two blocks hold the same energy whichever way you join them. Parallel strings share the load like any parallel paths. Their emfs are equal and they sit on the same busbars, so each path loses the same volts. Each current is those volts divided by its path's resistance. So each string takes current inversely to its resistance. Say two strings of 10 mΩ each share 100 A. One is on 2 mΩ of cable and the other on 6 mΩ. Their paths are 12 and 16 mΩ. So the first carries 100 × 16 ÷ 28 = 57 A, and the second 43 A. The string on the short cable works harder and is run down further. That is why makers ask for strings of the same capacity, design and age, with cables of equal resistance, and no more than four in parallel.[^3] The capacities and resistances here are examples. The tanks treat each cell's ampere-hours as fixed. They also count charge in as equal to charge out. **Cells in series share one current, so the weakest cell empties first on discharge, fills first when charged from flat, and is overdriven either way.**

analogy.text: Think of a radial circuit run partly in a smaller cable. The same current flows through every length. So the smallest cable sets what the whole circuit can carry. Push past that, and it is the one that overheats. A string works the same way. One current passes every cell. So the weakest cell sets what the string can give, and it is the one overdriven.
analogy.breaks: A cable stores nothing, so its limit is a current. A cell's limit is ampere-hours. So the weak cell mainly limits how long the string runs, not how hard. And a cable never turns round, but an emptied cell can be driven backwards.

practice.text:
Use this when you read a string, test it, or join strings in parallel.

- On float, read every cell's voltage, not only the total. The charger holds the total, so the total hides a bad cell.
- Compare each cell with its band. Say the float is 2.23 V a cell, with each cell allowed 0.05 V below to 0.10 V above it.
- Note any cell outside the band, high or low. On a vented cell, read its specific gravity too.
- Equalise when cells differ by more than about 0.10 V, or by more than 10 points of specific gravity.[^4] A cell 40 points away from the others is defective, and no equalise will cure it.
- On a discharge test, watch the cell voltages as well as the total. Then a weak cell shows before it is driven backwards.
- After an equalise or a boost, let the string stand for a few hours. Then read the odd cell again. A charge can cover a weak cell for a while. But the fault is likely to return within hours.
- Join strings in parallel only when they match in capacity, design and age. Join no more than four. Run each on cable of the same size and length. Then each path has the same resistance.

**Rule of thumb:** a series string gives the ampere-hours of its smallest cell. Parallel strings at equal voltage share the current inversely to their path resistance.

**Worked example:** A 12-cell string floats at 2.23 V a cell.[^1] So the charger holds 12 × 2.23 = 26.76 V. One cell reads 2.08 V. The other eleven share 26.76 − 2.08 = 24.68 V. That is about 2.24 V each. The total is right, and eleven cells look normal. But 2.08 V is 0.15 V below 2.23 V, which is outside the band. That cell is the one to chase.

**Common mistakes**
- Judging a string by its total voltage.
- Expecting a string to give the average of its cells' ampere-hours.
- Taking a good reading straight after a charge as proof a cell is cured.
- Running parallel strings on cables of different lengths.
- Thinking series or parallel changes how much energy two blocks hold.

sources.title: Flooded Stationary Lead Acid Batteries IOM — EnerSys
sources.quote: The recommended float / charge voltage is 2.23 V/cell remove per cell at 20°C (68°F) depending on the specific type (see table 5). The charger voltage amounts to Uflo per cell x no. of cells (tolerance ± 1 %).

sources.title: Flooded Stationary Lead Acid Batteries IOM — EnerSys
sources.quote: Deviations of individual cell voltages of –0.05 to +0.10 V/c may be observed. However the total voltage of the battery shall be within the limits stated above.

sources.title: Flooded Stationary Lead Acid Batteries IOM — EnerSys
sources.quote: In the case of parallel connected strings use batteries of the same capacity, design and age only with a maximum of 4 parallel strings. The resistance of the cables in each string must be the same, e.g. same cross-section, same length.

sources.title: Battery University | BU-803a: Cell Matching and Balancing
sources.quote: Manufacturers of golf cars, aerial work platforms, floor scrubbers and other battery-powered vehicles recommend an equalizing charge if the voltage difference between the cells is greater than +/– 0.10V, or if the specific gravity varies more than 10 points (0.010 on the SG scale).
